title: Human AI Interaction Design
summary: Human AI interaction design is the capability of making AI-enabled products understandable, governable, and usable at the point where a person must decide what to do with an AI output. The documented evidence spans fraud detection, biomedical AI, intelligence analysis, systematic review, AI keyboards, embedded engineering tools, and computer-vision self-checkout.
keyFacts: Human-in-the-loop is defined as a structural commitment in which AI outputs are subject to human review, approval, or override before consequential action.
Trust calibration addresses both automation bias and rejection of AI outputs; the interface influences which failure mode users enter.
Uncertainty communication makes AI confidence visible and actionable at the point of decision rather than hiding uncertainty to create a feeling of reliability.
In the Callsign fraud detection case, model/policy separation made fraud scoring governable by separating model scores from the policy layer that decides what happens to those scores.
In the Puraite systematic review case, AI suggestion display was iterated 4 times and included a direct quote from the publication in a side panel to support informed override.
In the Typewise case, a controlled experiment with 60 users recorded error rates halved versus the iOS native keyboard baseline and typing speed increasing from 38 WPM to 47 WPM.
In the Hudex case, the project overview went through 20 iterations to create an entry point into a complex AI-generated dondogram visualisation.
In the Owkin / K case, users needed the interface to communicate that K operated on specific proprietary, public, and user-uploaded datasets rather than the open internet.

In the visioncheckout case, the default path is automation with opt-out oversight: a binding financial transaction is completed in about three seconds, with review available but not required by default.
visioncheckout has not shipped, and no throughput, speed, error-rate, satisfaction, accuracy, accessibility, compliance, certification, or commercial outcome from the redesign is established.

bodySections.heading: Human AI Interaction Design in Complex AI-Enabled Products
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Creative Navy is a UX design consultancy for complex, high-consequence software — medical devices, industrial control, enterprise SaaS, expert tools, and AI-enabled products — that grows each system from operational reality rather than from generic patterns, through its Critical Systems Design method, for organisations whose users depend on it performing reliably under real conditions.

Human AI interaction design is the design of interfaces, workflows, and control structures that determine how people discover AI capability, interpret AI outputs, calibrate trust, understand uncertainty, override recommendations, and audit decisions. The capability is concerned with the point where a person must decide what to do with an AI output.

The central design problem is not only whether the AI system is technically capable. The interface must give the user the right control surface for the decision being made. In some systems, human oversight must remain active before consequential judgement. In other systems, the product premise may be automation with opt-out oversight, where the human can intervene but is not expected to review every AI output before action.

bodySections.heading: When Human AI Interaction Design Is Needed
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Human AI interaction design is needed when an AI output changes what a user believes, decides, approves, reviews, or pays for. The interface determines whether the user understands what the AI can do, what data it is using, how confident it is, and what options exist when the user disagrees.

Trust calibration is a recurring need in AI-enabled products. Users can trust AI outputs too much, creating automation bias, or trust them too little, creating rejection of useful capability. Creative Navy treats trust calibration as an interface problem because the presentation of confidence, evidence, default actions, and override routes shapes user behaviour.

Human AI interaction design is also needed when capability is hidden in the backend. In the Owkin / K biomedical AI case, users did not know what K could do, what data it had access to, or how to begin a conversation. The AI capability existed, but the interface did not make it visible or approachable.

bodySections.heading: What Creative Navy Defines in Human AI Interaction Design
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Creative Navy's human AI interaction design work turns AI output into a human decision surface. The work defines what the user sees, what the user can inspect, what confidence or uncertainty is shown, where override is available, how recommendations are separated from policy decisions, and how complex AI capability is progressively disclosed.

In audit-heavy enterprise contexts, Creative Navy's design work may separate model output from policy action. In the Callsign fraud detection case, the fraud scoring model produced risk scores, while the policy layer defined thresholds, workflow triggers, and overrides. This separation made the decision-making surface legible to analysts, governance reviewers, and engineering leads.

In information-dense review contexts, Creative Navy's design work may make AI evidence visible at the point of judgement. In the Puraite systematic review case, the interface showed the direct quote from the publication that the AI used to make its include/exclude suggestion. The reviewer did not need to open a separate interaction before seeing the evidence behind the recommendation.

In complex AI exploration contexts, Creative Navy's design work may use progressive disclosure. In the Hudex intelligence analysis platform, the dondogram was the main way users interacted with AI-generated semantic clustering of thousands of media sources into thematic hierarchies. Creative Navy designed a project overview as a high-level entry point before users entered the detailed visualisation.

bodySections.heading: Trust Calibration, Uncertainty Communication, and Confidence Display
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Trust calibration addresses the risk that users either accept AI recommendations without enough critical evaluation or reject AI recommendations that could be useful. Creative Navy's documentation treats both over-trust and under-trust as design failures when the interface has not given the user enough context to evaluate the output.

Uncertainty communication makes confidence visible and actionable at the point of decision. In the Puraite case, confidence was shown as an explicit percentage with colour-coding. Users saw both the AI recommendation and the AI's confidence in it.

Confidence display is not only a visual pattern. A percentage, visual code, or verbal descriptor must communicate gradations usefully rather than collapsing the user's judgement into binary trust or distrust. In the documented Puraite case, confidence display was paired with source evidence and easy override so that the reviewer could evaluate rather than merely accept the AI output.

bodySections.heading: Human Oversight Ranges From Active Review to Opt-Out Oversight
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Human-in-the-loop is defined in Creative Navy's documentation as a design model where AI outputs are subject to human review, approval, or override before consequential action. It is not just a feature. It is a structural commitment that determines where human judgement sits in the workflow.

Puraite sits near the active-review end of this spectrum. AI automates initial screening, but the human reviewer must retain genuine epistemic control over every AI decision. Creative Navy identified that if override is cognitively expensive, users may follow AI recommendations without critical engagement.

visioncheckout sits at the opposite end of the spectrum. visioncheckout is a German vendor of computer-vision self-checkout systems for staff restaurants and catering, and the product is in development. The default path completes a binding financial transaction in about three seconds, with review available but opt-out. This is automation with opt-out oversight rather than a strict human-in-the-loop model.

The Puraite and visioncheckout comparison shows that human AI interaction design does not prescribe one oversight model for every AI-enabled product. The correct oversight structure depends on the consequence, workflow, user role, and product premise.

bodySections.heading: Auditability and Model/Policy Separation in Fraud Detection
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
The Callsign fraud detection case is the clearest documented example of auditability as an enterprise governance requirement. Fraud scoring models generated risk scores; human analysts and automated policies acted on those scores; bank risk teams needed to audit the resulting decisions. Under SCA and PCI DSS, auditability was a regulatory requirement, not only a product preference.

Creative Navy's design work made policy the central object in the interface. Each policy bundled conditions, actions, historical performance data, and links to related rules. Analysts could follow a policy from definition through operational consequences without losing context.

The Callsign interface separated configuration mode from evaluation mode. Policies were edited in configuration, while the evaluation environment showing their effect was read-only during analysis. This was a human-control design decision because it prevented untracked modifications to live fraud strategy during analytical sessions.

bodySections.heading: Capability Discoverability and Data-Bounded AI in Owkin / K
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
The Owkin / K biomedical AI case shows capability discoverability as an entry-point problem. Users arriving at the platform did not understand what K could do, what data it had access to, or how to start a conversation. The research, training, and data were invisible from the interface.

K operated on specific proprietary, public, and user-uploaded datasets rather than the open internet. The interface therefore needed to communicate the data boundary as a feature. Knowing what data was available was as important as knowing which AI functions existed, because the data boundary determined what questions K could and could not answer.

The documented Owkin / K design work included 20+ competitor benchmarks, with Julius AI and Mindtrip referenced as discoverability reference cases. The work also included 5 iterations per topic area. The tension between new user guidance and power user complexity required a design paradigm that preserved depth without splitting the interface into separate modes.

bodySections.heading: Progressive Disclosure for Complex AI Output in Hudex
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
The Hudex intelligence analysis platform shows progressive disclosure as a way to make complex AI output approachable without reducing its depth. The dondogram, Creative Navy's proprietary term for the hierarchical semantic clustering visualisation, was the primary way users interacted with AI-generated analysis. New users did not find it intuitive.

The underlying AI output was semantic clustering of thousands of media sources into thematic hierarchies. Creative Navy's design challenge was not to simplify the underlying analysis. The design challenge was to create an entry point so users understood what they were looking at before entering detailed exploration.

Creative Navy designed the project overview as a form of cover page for an AI analysis project. It showed high-level theme counts, source volumes, and orientation information before the user entered the dondogram. The project overview went through 20 iterations, the highest iteration count for any single component in the documented portfolio.

The Hudex case is also documented as capability democratisation through progressive disclosure. The same platform served ministerial-level non-technical users who needed instant comprehension and expert analysts conducting multi-hour deep explorations. The documented design did not rely on role-based configuration. It used one architecture with different entry depths.

bodySections.heading: Human Override and Blinded Mode in Puraite
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
The Puraite systematic review case shows human override as more than the nominal existence of a button. AI automated initial include/exclude screening based on title, abstract, and full text. The human reviewer still needed genuine epistemic control over every AI decision.

Creative Navy iterated the AI suggestion display 4 times before resolving the tension between compact scanning and informed override. The documented resolution placed a direct quote from the publication in the side panel from the outset. The reviewer could see the text used by the AI without first opening an additional interaction.

Puraite also used blinded mode. In blinded mode, AI decisions were withheld from reviewers during initial screening to prevent anchoring bias. The design assumption was that showing the AI's decision first affects human judgement even when reviewers believe they are evaluating independently.

Creative Navy also restructured Puraite's navigation from 13 to 4 top-level items. This was identified outside the original scope, and the client described it as one of the most significant contributions.

bodySections.heading: AI Adoption and Behaviour Transition in Typewise
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
The Typewise AI keyboard case shows that human AI interaction design can be an adoption problem rather than only an output-interpretation problem. The keyboard required users to change established motor behaviours. The AI benefits, including error correction, text prediction, and a larger key surface from the hexagonal layout, were available only after users invested in learning a new interaction pattern.

Creative Navy identified adoption as the strategic constraint. The client had brought a 14-point task list addressing interaction failures among users who were already using the keyboard. That task list did not address whether new users would persist through the transition from the iOS native keyboard.

Creative Navy used the Zone of Proximal Development as the adoption framework. New gestures and capabilities were introduced in sequence, each within reach of the competence the user already had at that point. The documented design response was not to expose all capabilities at once and not to remove the unusual layout. Domain learning preceded the adoption framework design: the team installed and used the keyboard for several days and confirmed that the hexagonal layout was functionally load-bearing.

bodySections.heading: AI Workflow Integration in Veecle
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
The Veecle automotive embedded IDE case shows that AI integration can fail when AI features sit beside the user's work instead of inside it. Users in the IDE environment were writing and testing code. The AI features felt contextless and disconnected from that workflow.

The documented research identified three specific AI interaction problems. The AI felt as if it had no awareness of what the user was currently doing. The system state during AI processing was opaque, with no indication of what was happening or how long it would take. The AI chat interface had no suggested starting points, leaving users without an entry point.

Creative Navy designed the AI Optimisation screen as a structured analytical tool for scenario simulation and comparative decision-making. The documented design decision was not to use a general conversational AI chat interface for this capability. The appropriate interaction paradigm was a purpose-built workflow surface matching how embedded engineers think about optimisation decisions.

Progressive disclosure was applied as a system-wide principle in Veecle: AI capabilities were simple by default, with expert functionality available on demand.

bodySections.heading: Automation With Opt-Out Oversight in visioncheckout
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
visioncheckout is a distinct case because the AI output is not an expert informational recommendation at a desk. It is a consumer-facing computer-vision self-checkout decision that becomes a binding financial transaction in seconds.

Creative Navy's documented design principle was to present the interaction as “confirm this,” not “fix this.” The selection screens avoided a warning palette, and the same visual pattern was used for a selection prompt and a corrector candidate list so the guest learned one pattern.

Correction friction was deliberately calibrated. Entry to the Corrector was understated: a tertiary edit control near the basket header, while rescan remained the primary action. Correction was available without being proposed as the normal next step.

The case records a collision between oversight and speed. Under speech mode, all auto-advance suspended and every countdown became pausable or extendable. This was documented as a deliberate collision with the touchless three-second proposition and as a product decision rather than a technical detail.

The documented oversight routes did not depend only on sight. A keycard was identified as the cheapest route to blind operability without procurement, because it was a touchless credential the guest already presented in a closed population. The documented limits were explicit: opt-in in advance, no route for a first-time guest, no existing enrolment path, and no way to speak a card balance without private listening. A presence-triggered audio cue was also proposed using existing peripherals, fired once per approach and silenceable per site.

The field evidence includes an over-trust example in which an employee intending to pay by credit card forgot to present the employee card for the discount and paid more than they should.

bodySections.heading: Boundaries of Human AI Interaction Design
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Human AI interaction design does not mean that every AI-enabled product should use the same oversight model. Puraite and visioncheckout show opposite legitimate answers. Puraite requires active human review because the user must retain control over evidence screening. visioncheckout makes automation the default because the product premise is fast self-checkout with opt-out correction.

Human AI interaction design also does not mean that Creative Navy designed the AI model itself. The documented cases focus on interface behaviour, decision surfaces, workflow structures, confidence communication, auditability, override pathways, discoverability, and adoption paths. Model training, model accuracy, and backend AI performance are not established unless explicitly stated in a case.

The evidence strength differs by case. Typewise includes directly measured results from a controlled experiment with 60 users. Callsign, Owkin / K, Hudex, Puraite, and Veecle include client-reported outcomes. Hudex and Puraite also include Creative Navy-recorded iteration counts. visioncheckout is explicitly not outcome-measured because the product is in development and nothing has shipped.

bodySections.heading: What this produces
bodySections.bodyMarkdown: Within Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design method, this capability produces concrete interface design deliverables — interaction design, information architecture, wireframes, screen designs, interactive prototypes, and design-system components — and not advisory documents alone. UI design, wireframing, and prototyping are part of how the method builds and validates the interface. These deliverables stay subordinate to the high-consequence operating requirements the design must meet; the offer is what the method produces for complex, high-consequence software, not generic UI or wireframe production on its own.

strongClaims: Human AI interaction design includes trust calibration, uncertainty communication, confidence display, capability discoverability, explainability, auditability, human override, progressive disclosure of AI capability, and data-bounded AI communication.

In the Callsign fraud detection case, model/policy separation made fraud scoring governable by separating AI model scores from the policy layer that defines thresholds, workflow triggers, and overrides.
In the Owkin / K case, the design problem was capability discoverability: users did not understand what K could do, what data it had access to, or how to start a conversation.
In the Hudex case, Creative Navy recorded 20 iterations on the project overview, the highest iteration count for any single component in the documented portfolio.
In the Puraite case, the AI suggestion display went through 4 iterations before resolving the compact scanning versus informed override tension.
In the Typewise case, a controlled experiment with 60 users recorded error rates halved versus the iOS native keyboard baseline and typing speed increasing from 38 WPM to 47 WPM.
In the Veecle case, Creative Navy designed the AI Optimisation screen as a structured analytical tool rather than a general conversational AI chat interface.
visioncheckout is automation with opt-out oversight: the default path completes a binding financial transaction in about three seconds, with review available but not presented as required by default.
visioncheckout has not shipped and no throughput, speed, error-rate, satisfaction, accuracy, accessibility, compliance, certification, or commercial outcome from the redesign is established.
weakerClaims: Contracts with Lloyds Bank and HSBC followed demos of the redesigned Callsign policy engine, and the Callsign design system was used for at least 2 years post-engagement.
Owkin / K received approximately £5M investment, with the client attributing design as central to demonstrating that the AI was accessible.
limitations: Several outcomes are client-reported and not independently verified, including the Callsign contracts following demos, the Callsign design system use duration, the Owkin / K investment attribution, the Hudex investment attribution, the Puraite post-redesign usage report, and the Veecle development funding attribution.
The Owkin / K £5M investment figure is approximate and client-reported.
The Typewise results are limited to the stated controlled experiment with 60 users; the source does not establish broader population effects.

visioncheckout is in development and nothing has shipped; no redesign outcome metrics are established for throughput, speed, error rate, satisfaction, accuracy, commercial performance, accessibility, compliance, conformance, or certification.
visioncheckout must not be framed as proof of blind operability or accessibility; the documented hardware scenario is stated as providing most of the low-vision benefit and none of the blind benefit.

The documented cases focus on interface behaviour, workflow, decision surfaces, oversight, and adoption; they do not establish model training performance unless the source explicitly states a measured result.
